title: Topologies without distance
objectives: Check the topology axioms, including spaces with no metric.

screens.title: One set is missing
screens.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c\}$ we want a family of "open" sets, with no distance at all. The solid sets $\varnothing$, $\{a\}$, $\{b\}$ and $X$ are in the family; dashed sets are not. We want every union of members to be a member.

state.caption: Lines join a set to the sets just above it.

screens.question: Tap the one set that must be added so that every union of members is a member.

hints.text: Take the union of two members.
Try $\{a\} \cup \{b\}$.
$\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}$, which is dashed.

feedback.correct: Right. With $\{a, b\}$ added, every union and intersection is a member.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Form every union of two solid sets.

byKey.c: $\{c\}$ is no union of members: no member holds $c$ except $X$.
byKey.ac: $\{a, c\}$ is no union of members, since no member other than $X$ holds $c$.
byKey.bc: $\{b, c\}$ is no union of members, since no member other than $X$ holds $c$.

explain.text: $\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}$ was missing. With it the family $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ is closed under unions and intersections.

screens.title: Unions and intersections
screens.prose: Now take the family $\{\varnothing, \{a, b\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$. Each cell shows the union ($\cup$) and intersection ($\cap$) of its row and column sets. Here X is $\{a, b, c\}$.
screens.question: Tap every cell whose union or intersection is not in the family.

hints.text: The family's members are ∅, ab, bc and X.
Look at ab against bc.
$\{a, b\} \cap \{b, c\} = \{b\}$ is missing, in two cells.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read each cell's two results against the four members.

byKey.r3c2: You missed the second cell. The table is symmetric, so $\{b, c\} \cap \{a, b\}$ fails too.
byKey.r2c2: $\{a, b\} \cup \{a, b\} = \{a, b\}$ is a member.

explain.text: Every union is a member, but $\{a, b\} \cap \{b, c\} = \{b\}$ is not. So this family fails the intersection rule.

screens.title: The axioms
screens.prose: A **topology** on $X$ is a family $\tau$ of subsets, the **open sets**. It must satisfy: $$\varnothing, X \in \tau; \quad \textstyle\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha \in \tau \text{ for any } U_\alpha \in \tau; \quad U \cap V \in \tau \text{ for } U, V \in \tau.$$ Level 1 showed that metric open sets obey all three.
screens.question: Which axiom did the family $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b\}, X\}$ of the first screen break?

options.text: Unions: $\{a\} \cup \{b\}$ was missing.
Finite intersections.
options.why: $\{a\} \cap \{b\} = \varnothing$, which is a member. The failure was a union.

options.text: $\varnothing$ and $X$ must belong.
options.why: Both were solid on the first screen.

hints.text: Which set did you add?

feedback.correct: Right. The second screen's family broke the third axiom.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall the set you added on the first screen.

explain.text: We added $\{a, b\} = \{a\} \cup \{b\}$, so the union axiom failed. On the second screen the intersection axiom failed instead.

screens.title: Three candidates
screens.question: Which families are topologies? Select all that apply.

options.text: A
B
options.why: $\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}$ is missing, as on the first screen.

options.text: C
options.why: $\{a, b\} \cap \{b, c\} = \{b\}$ is missing, as on the second screen.

hints.text: Check every pair in each family.
A is a chain: each set holds the one before, so unions and intersections stay inside.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each union and each intersection of two members.

explain.text: A is a chain $\varnothing \subset \{a\} \subset \{a, b\} \subset X$, so every union and intersection is a member. B fails a union and C fails an intersection. The **discrete** topology (every subset) and the **indiscrete** one ($\varnothing$ and $X$ only) are the extremes.

screens.title: How many topologies?
screens.prose: On a one-point set there is exactly one topology. Now take $X = \{a, b\}$, with four subsets.
screens.question: How many topologies are there on $\{a, b\}$?

widget.accept: 4: indiscrete, discrete, and $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, X\}$ and $\{\varnothing, \{b\}, X\}$.

hints.text: $\varnothing$ and $X$ are forced. Which of $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ may you add?
Any choice works: neither, either, or both.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Decide separately whether $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ are open.

byKey.two: You kept only the discrete and indiscrete topologies. $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, X\}$ is a topology too.
byKey.three: You counted one space with a single point open. $\{a\}$ open and $\{b\}$ open are two different topologies.
byKey.all: 16 counts every family of subsets. Each must contain $\varnothing$ and $X$.

explain.text: With $\varnothing$ and $X$ forced, any choice of $\{a\}$ and $\{b\}$ satisfies the axioms. That gives 4: the two **Sierpiński** spaces, the discrete and the indiscrete. There are 29 on three points and 355 on four.

screens.title: Metric spaces separate points
screens.prose: In a metric space, take two points $x \ne y$. We show they have disjoint open balls, so the space is **Hausdorff**. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose some $z$ lies in both $B(x, r)$ and $B(y, r)$.
Then $d(x, y) \le d(x, z) + d(z, y) < r + r = d(x, y)$, by the triangle inequality.
That is impossible, so the balls are disjoint open sets round $x$ and $y$. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: The balls may overlap: in $\mathbb{R}$, $B(0, 1)$ and $B(1, 1)$ share $(0, 1)$.

hints.text: Half the distance leaves a gap.
Assume a common point and reach $d(x, y) < d(x, y)$.

feedback.correct: Right. Half the distance keeps the balls apart.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the radius, then assume a common point.

byKey.d1: You used the whole distance. The balls can then overlap, as $B(0, 1)$ and $B(1, 1)$ do in $\mathbb{R}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: With $r = \tfrac{d(x, y)}{2}$, a common point would give $d(x, y) < d(x, y)$. So every metric space is Hausdorff: distinct points have disjoint open sets round them.

screens.title: A space with no metric
screens.prose: The **Sierpiński space** is $\{0, 1\}$ with open sets $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$ and $\{0, 1\}$.
screens.question: Why can no metric give exactly these open sets?

options.text: The only open set holding 0 is $\{0, 1\}$, which also holds 1. So 0 and 1 have no disjoint open sets.
Two points are too few for a metric.
options.why: The discrete metric works on two points; its open sets are all four subsets.

options.text: $\{0\}$ is missing, and every topology must contain the singletons.
options.why: Topologies need not contain singletons: the indiscrete one has none. The failure is the Hausdorff property.

hints.text: Use the proof you just ordered.
Which open sets contain 0?
Only $\{0, 1\}$, which meets every open set round 1.

feedback.correct: Right. Metric spaces are Hausdorff; this space is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List the open sets that contain 0.

explain.text: A metric would separate 0 and 1 by disjoint balls. Here every open set round 0 is $\{0, 1\}$, which contains 1. So the space is not Hausdorff and no metric gives its open sets.

screens.title: The cofinite topology
screens.prose: On $\mathbb{Z}$ call $U$ open when $U = \varnothing$ or $\mathbb{Z} \setminus U$ is finite. This is the **cofinite** topology.

state.caption: $U = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{-2, 1, 3\}$ is open: it leaves out three points.

screens.question: Why is the cofinite topology on $\mathbb{Z}$ not Hausdorff?

options.text: Two non-empty open sets each leave out finitely many points, so they always meet.
Non-empty finite sets are not open.
options.why: True, but that alone does not stop separation. The point is that open sets are too big to be disjoint.

options.text: It is not a topology: a union of open sets can leave out infinitely many points.
options.why: A union of non-empty open sets leaves out fewer points, not more. It is a topology.

hints.text: Can two sets with finite complements be disjoint in an infinite set?
$U \cap V$ leaves out at most the points $U$ or $V$ leave out, a finite number.

feedback.correct: Right. Any two non-empty open sets meet.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does $U \cap V$ leave out?

explain.text: $\mathbb{Z} \setminus (U \cap V) = (\mathbb{Z} \setminus U) \cup (\mathbb{Z} \setminus V)$ is finite, so $U \cap V$ is infinite. Disjoint non-empty open sets cannot exist, so no metric gives this topology.

screens.title: Complements are not required
screens.prose: A learner who knows probability rejects $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ on $X = \{a, b, c\}$. "$\{a\}$ is open but its complement $\{b, c\}$ is not, so $\tau$ fails."
screens.question: Who is right?

options.text: $\tau$ is a topology. The axioms ask for unions and finite intersections, not complements.
The learner: open sets must be closed under complements.
options.why: You mixed a topology up with a $\sigma$-algebra of events, which must hold complements. A topology need not.

options.text: The learner: every open set must also be closed.
options.why: That holds only in special spaces, such as discrete ones. In $\mathbb{R}$, $(0, 1)$ is open and not closed.

hints.text: Reread the three axioms.
$\tau$ is a chain.
Complements are a rule for $\sigma$-algebras, not topologies.

feedback.correct: Right. Open sets need not have open complements.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check $\tau$ against the three axioms only.

byKey.sigma: You used the rule for events. A $\sigma$-algebra needs complements; a topology needs unions and finite intersections.

explain.text: $\tau$ is a chain, so it holds every union and intersection of its members. The complement rule belongs to $\sigma$-algebras, which `measure-prob` builds. In $\mathbb{R}$ the open set $(0, 1)$ has a complement that is not open.

screens.title: The smallest spaces
screens.prose: The axioms still apply when $X$ is tiny. On the empty set, $\varnothing$ and $X$ are the same set.
screens.question: How many topologies are there on the empty set?

hints.text: Which families of subsets of $\varnothing$ are there?
Only $\{\}$ and $\{\varnothing\}$; the axioms need $\varnothing \in \tau$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The family must contain $\varnothing = X$.

byKey.none: You assumed the empty set has no topology. $\{\varnothing\}$ meets every axiom.
byKey.two: The empty family fails: it must contain $\varnothing$.

explain.text: The only subset of $\varnothing$ is $\varnothing$, which is also $X$. So $\tau = \{\varnothing\}$ is forced, and it is the one topology. The count runs 1, 1, 4, 29 for 0 to 3 points.

screens.title: Checking the axioms by machine
screens.prose: Write `is_topology(X, tau)` for a set `X` and a list of frozensets. Then `count_topologies(n)` counts topologies on `range(n)` by brute force over families. The hidden helper `T('', 'a', 'ab')` builds a family. Checking cases is evidence, not proof.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests, compared exactly. Seven test is_topology: the three candidates, a family missing ∅, the discrete topology, and two four-point families (one fails only $\{a, b\} \cap \{b, c\}$). Four count topologies on 0 to 3 points. The first Check starts Python in the browser, about 4 s once.

hints.text: For a finite family, checking every pair covers every union and intersection.
Count by running over every bit mask of the $2^n$ subsets.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check $\varnothing$, $X$, and every pair's union and intersection.

explain.text: On a finite set, closure under pairs gives closure under every union and intersection. The brute force gives 1, 1, 4 and 29; four points give 355, too slow to test here.

screens.title: Alerts you can confirm
screens.prose: Each desk alert is a set of market states. In those states it fires, and a check confirms it in finite time. "The price touched £110" can be confirmed once it happens. "The price never touches £110" never can.

rows: every one of infinitely many fires

screens.question: What structure do the confirmable statements form?

options.text: A topology: closed under any union and finite intersections, but not complements
A $\sigma$-algebra, since they are events
options.why: A $\sigma$-algebra needs complements. "Never fires" is the complement of an alert and cannot be confirmed.

options.text: Every set of states, the discrete topology
options.why: "Never touches £110" is a set of states that no finite check confirms.

hints.text: Which rows are yes?
Unions and finite intersections yes; infinite intersections and complements no.

feedback.correct: Right. Confirmable statements behave like open sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Match the yes rows to the axioms.

explain.text: Any union is confirmed when one alert fires, and a finite intersection when each has fired. Infinite intersections and complements may need forever. That is a topology, not a $\sigma$-algebra.

ideas: A topology on $X$ contains $\varnothing$, $X$, every union of members and every finite intersection. There are 1, 4, 29 and 355 on 1 to 4 points.
Every metric space is Hausdorff: radius $\tfrac{d(x, y)}{2}$ separates two points. The Sierpiński space and the cofinite topology on $\mathbb{Z}$ are not, so no metric gives them.
A topology need not contain complements; that is the rule for a $\sigma$-algebra.

formula.name: Topology axioms
formula.note: Any unions, finite intersections, no complements.

summary.trap: Rejecting $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ because $\{b, c\}$ is missing confuses a topology with a $\sigma$-algebra.

quiz.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c, d\}$ take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, \{a, b, c\}, X\}$.
quiz.question: Is $\tau$ a topology?

options.text: Yes: it is a chain, so unions and intersections are members
No: the complement $\{b, c, d\}$ of $\{a\}$ is missing
options.why: Complements are not required in a topology.

options.text: No: the singletons $\{b\}$, $\{c\}$, $\{d\}$ are missing
options.why: Singletons need not be open; the indiscrete topology has none.

feedback.correct: Right. Any chain from $\varnothing$ to $X$ is a topology.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the three axioms only.

explain.text: In a chain the union of two members is the larger and the intersection the smaller. Both are members, so $\tau$ is a topology.

quiz.prose: We counted 4 topologies on two points.
quiz.question: How many topologies are there on three points?

widget.accept: 29, by brute force over the 64 families that contain ∅ and X.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall the count the code gave for $n = 3$.

byKey.fam: 64 counts every family holding $\varnothing$ and $X$. Most break an axiom.
byKey.eight: 8 counts subsets of $\{a, b, c\}$, not families of them.

explain.text: Of the $2^6 = 64$ families that contain $\varnothing$ and $X$, exactly 29 are closed under unions and intersections. The sequence runs 1, 1, 4, 29, 355.

quiz.prose: Let $X$ be a finite set with a Hausdorff topology.
quiz.question: Which topology must it be?

options.text: The discrete topology
The indiscrete topology
options.why: With two or more points, the only open set round each point is $X$, so they cannot be separated.

options.text: Any topology at all
options.why: The Sierpiński space is finite and not Hausdorff.

feedback.correct: Right. Every singleton is then open.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Intersect the open sets that separate $x$ from each other point.

explain.text: For each $y \ne x$ pick an open $U_y \ni x$ missing $y$. The finite intersection of the $U_y$ is $\{x\}$, so every singleton is open and the topology is discrete.
